unit.name: Data
unit.subtitle: Binary, two's complement, hexadecimal, character encoding, images, sound, storage units and compression

lessons.title: Binary Numbers, Two's Complement and Hexadecimal
lessons.description: Positive and negative integers in binary, two's complement, and hexadecimal notation.
lessons.content_html:
Why Computers Use Binary

Every piece of data inside a computer — text, images, sound, instructions — is stored and processed as a pattern of 1s and 0s. This is the binary (base-2) number system. A transistor in a chip is either conducting electricity or not — that two-state physical reality maps perfectly onto binary’s two digits. A bit is a single binary digit. Eight bits make one byte.

The number of distinct states that can be represented by a binary pattern of a given length is always a power of 2. One bit gives 2 states (0 or 1). Two bits give 4 states (00, 01, 10, 11). Eight bits give \(2^8 = 256\) states. In general, \(n\) bits can represent \(2^n\) different values.

Key Fact

An 8-bit binary number has place values 128 — 64 — 32 — 16 — 8 — 4 — 2 — 1 (left to right). To convert binary to denary, add up the place values where the digit is 1. The maximum unsigned 8-bit value is 11111111 = 255; the minimum is 00000000 = 0.

Converting Between Binary and Denary

Denary (decimal) uses place values that are powers of 10. Binary uses powers of 2. Converting binary to denary means reading off the place values where a 1 appears and adding them together.

Binary → Denary: Convert 10110101

Place values: 128  64  32  16  8  4  2  1
Bits:          1     0    1    1    0   1   0   1
Values that count: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 181

Denary → Binary: Convert 203
128 fits: 203 − 128 = 75, write 1
64 fits: 75 − 64 = 11, write 1
32 does not fit in 11, write 0
16 does not fit in 11, write 0
8 fits: 11 − 8 = 3, write 1
4 does not fit in 3, write 0
2 fits: 3 − 2 = 1, write 1
1 fits: 1 − 1 = 0, write 1
Result: 11001011
Check: 128 + 64 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 203 ✓

Two’s Complement — Representing Negative Numbers

Unsigned binary can only represent positive integers and zero. To store negative integers, computers use two’s complement. In 8-bit two’s complement, the most significant bit (leftmost bit) has a place value of −128 instead of +128. The remaining seven bits retain their normal positive place values.

This means 8-bit two’s complement can represent integers from −128 to +127. Positive numbers look the same as unsigned binary — the most significant bit is 0. Negative numbers have the most significant bit set to 1.

Key Fact

In 8-bit two’s complement the place values are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The range is −128 to +127. To convert a negative pattern to denary, treat the leftmost bit as −128 and add the remaining place values as normal.

How to represent −5 in 8-bit two’s complement:

Step 1 — Write +5 in 8-bit binary: 00000101

Step 2 — Invert all bits (flip every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0): 11111010

Step 3 — Add 1 to the result: 11111010 + 00000001 = 11111011

Check: Using place value −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −128 + 123 = −5 ✓

Converting 10010011 back to denary:
Place value of leftmost bit = −128
Remaining bits 0010011: 16 + 2 + 1 = 19
Total: −128 + 19 = −109

Hexadecimal

Hexadecimal (hex, base-16) uses 16 symbols: digits 0–9 and letters A–F, where A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15. Hex is used because it is a compact shorthand for binary: every four bits (one nibble) maps to exactly one hex digit, making long binary strings much easier for humans to read.

You will see hex everywhere in computing: web colour codes (#FF5500), MAC addresses on network cards, memory dump listings in diagnostic tools. The maximum 8-bit value is FF in hex (255 in denary). Computers do not process hex directly — it is a human convenience for working with binary patterns.

Binary → Hex: Convert 11010110
Split into nibbles: 1101 | 0110
1101 = 13 = D
0110 = 6
Result: D6

Hex → Binary: Convert 3A
3 = 0011
A = 10 = 1010
Result: 00111010

Hex → Denary: Convert 3A
(3 × 16) + 10 = 48 + 10 = 58

Key Fact

To convert binary to hex: split into groups of 4 bits (nibbles) from the right, then convert each nibble to its hex digit. To convert hex to denary: multiply the first digit by 16, add the second digit. Hexadecimal is used in computing because one hex digit represents exactly four binary bits — making large binary numbers compact and readable.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For two’s complement questions, always show three clear steps: write the positive binary, invert all bits, add 1. The examiner awards method marks for each step shown. When converting a two’s complement pattern to denary, remember the leftmost bit has the place value −128, not +128 — a very common error. For hex conversion, the command word will often be ‘Convert’ (2 marks) — show the nibble split and both hex digits to secure full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Binary is base-2. An 8-bit number can represent \(2^8 = 256\) distinct values. Unsigned range is 0–255; two’s complement signed range is −128 to +127.
  • To represent a negative number in two’s complement: write the positive version, invert all bits, add 1. The leftmost bit carries place value −128.
  • Hexadecimal is base-16. Each hex digit represents exactly one nibble (4 bits). Convert binary to hex by splitting into nibbles and converting each group.

lessons.title: Binary Arithmetic and Shifts
lessons.description: Adding binary numbers, applying logical and arithmetic shifts, and recognising overflow.
lessons.content_html:
Binary Addition

Adding two binary numbers follows four simple rules. Applying these column by column from right to left gives the result:

  • 0 + 0 = 0
  • 1 + 0 = 1
  • 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1)
  • 1 + 1 + 1 (carry) = 11 (write 1, carry 1)

The carry bit moves one column to the left, just as it does in denary addition. Always work right to left, recording each sum digit and carrying any overflow to the next column.

Add 01101100 (108) and 00110101 (53):

  01101100
+ 00110101
----------

Working right to left:
Col 1 (1s): 0+1 = 1
Col 2 (2s): 0+0 = 0
Col 3 (4s): 1+1 = 0, carry 1
Col 4 (8s): 1+0+carry1 = 0, carry 1
Col 5 (16s): 0+1+carry1 = 0, carry 1
Col 6 (32s): 1+1+carry1 = 1, carry 1
Col 7 (64s): 1+0+carry1 = 0, carry 1
Col 8 (128s): 0+0+carry1 = 1
Result: 10100001
Check: 108 + 53 = 161; 10100001 = 128 + 32 + 1 = 161 ✓

Key Fact

Binary addition rules: 0+0=0; 1+0=1; 1+1=0 carry 1; 1+1+1(carry)=1 carry 1. Always work right to left. Show the carry row clearly in your working — examiners award method marks for visible carries.

Overflow

Overflow happens when the result of an addition exceeds the maximum value that can be stored in the available bit width. For 8-bit unsigned arithmetic, the maximum storable value is 255. If the addition produces a carry out from the leftmost (most significant) bit, the result cannot fit in 8 bits and overflow has occurred.

For example, adding 11000000 (192) and 01000001 (65) produces a carry beyond the 8th bit. The 8-bit result is incorrect — the true total of 257 cannot be stored in 8 bits. In a real computer, this causes an error state or silent data corruption depending on the hardware design.

Key Fact

Overflow occurs when an arithmetic result is too large for the number of bits available. In 8-bit unsigned addition, overflow happens when the true result exceeds 255 — a carry bit is produced beyond the eighth bit position and the stored result is incorrect.

Binary Shifts — Logical and Arithmetic

A binary shift moves every bit a stated number of positions left or right. There are two types: logical and arithmetic. Both left-shift by the same rules, but they differ when shifting right.

Logical Shifts

In a logical shift, every vacated bit position is filled with 0. A logical left shift by 1 moves every bit one place to the left, fills the rightmost position with 0, and loses the leftmost bit. A logical right shift by 1 moves every bit one place to the right, fills the leftmost position with 0, and loses the rightmost bit.

Effect on value: a logical left shift by \(n\) places multiplies the number by \(2^n\). A logical right shift by \(n\) places divides the number by \(2^n\) (integer division — remainder is lost). Example: 00001100 (12) logical-left-shifted by 2 gives 00110000 = 48. Check: \(12 \times 4 = 48\) ✓.

Arithmetic Shifts

An arithmetic shift is designed for use with two’s complement signed numbers. The key difference from a logical shift is in a right arithmetic shift: the sign bit (the most significant bit) is preserved — the vacated position on the left is filled with a copy of the sign bit, not with 0.

An arithmetic left shift works identically to a logical left shift — vacated positions are filled with 0. For positive numbers (where the sign bit is 0), an arithmetic right shift and a logical right shift produce the same result. The difference only appears for negative numbers, where the sign bit is 1.

Start with the 8-bit pattern 11110000. As a two’s complement signed integer: −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = −16.

Logical right shift by 2:
Vacated positions filled with 0: 00111100
Denary value: 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 60
Result is now positive — the sign has changed. The logical shift ignores the sign bit and treats the pattern as unsigned.

Arithmetic right shift by 2:
Sign bit is 1, so vacated positions on the left are filled with 1: 11111100
Denary value: −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = −4
Check: −16 ÷ 4 = −4 ✓. The arithmetic shift preserves the sign and correctly divides the signed value by \(2^2\).

Key Fact

Logical right shift: always fills vacated positions with 0. Treats the number as unsigned. Arithmetic right shift: fills vacated positions with a copy of the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative). Preserves the sign of two’s complement numbers. Both left shifts work the same way — filling with 0.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering shift questions, always state whether the shift is logical or arithmetic and always show the vacated bit positions explicitly. For an arithmetic right shift on a negative number, remember the vacated positions fill with 1 (copying the sign bit), not with 0. Overflow questions will ask you to ‘explain’ or ‘describe’ — link the concept to the specific number of bits available and what happens when the result exceeds that limit.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Binary addition uses four rules working right to left with carry bits. Show your carries clearly — method marks depend on visible working.
  • Overflow occurs when the result of an addition is too large for the available number of bits. In 8-bit unsigned arithmetic this means the result exceeds 255.
  • Logical shifts fill all vacated positions with 0. Arithmetic right shifts fill vacated positions with a copy of the sign bit, preserving the sign of two’s complement numbers. Both left shifts fill with 0.

lessons.title: Characters, Images and Sound
lessons.description: Encoding text with 7-bit ASCII and representing bitmap images and sampled sound in binary.
lessons.content_html:
How Computers Store Text

A computer stores everything as binary — including the letters you type. To do this, every character must be assigned a unique number, which is then stored as its binary equivalent. A character set is the agreed list that maps each character to its code. Without a shared standard, a file created on one system would display differently on another.

7-Bit ASCII

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) uses 7 bits per character, allowing \(2^7 = 128\) unique codes (0 to 127). These 128 characters cover upper-case letters, lower-case letters, the digit characters 0–9, punctuation marks and control characters such as “new line”.

The key principle is that codes are sequential within each group. Upper-case A = 65, B = 66, up to Z = 90. Lower-case a = 97, b = 98, up to z = 122. Digit character ‘0’ = 48, ‘1’ = 49, up to ‘9’ = 57. This sequential grouping means you can calculate any character’s code if you know one code in the same group.

Key Fact

In ASCII: upper-case A = 65; lower-case a = 97; digit character ‘0’ = 48. Codes are sequential: ‘P’ = 65 + 15 = 80; ‘m’ = 97 + 12 = 109. ASCII uses 7 bits and represents 128 characters.

Example 1: Given A = 65, what is the code for K?
K is the 11th letter. K = 65 + (11 − 1) = 65 + 10 = 75.

Example 2: A character has ASCII code 104. Given a = 97, what character is it?
104 − 97 = 7. Count 7 letters on from a: b, c, d, e, f, g, h.

Example 3: Given ‘0’ = 48, what is the binary for the character ‘5’?
‘5’ = 48 + 5 = 53. 53 in binary: 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 0110101.

Bitmap Images

Every digital image is built from a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels. Each pixel stores a single colour value in binary. The total number of pixels is determined by the image’s resolution — its width in pixels multiplied by its height in pixels.

Colour depth determines how many different colours are available per pixel. With 1-bit colour depth, only 2 colours are possible. With 8-bit depth, \(2^8 = 256\) colours are possible. With 24-bit depth, over 16 million distinct colours can be represented, appearing photorealistic to the human eye.

Key Fact

Image file size (bits) = width (pixels) × height (pixels) × colour depth (bits). To convert to bytes, divide by 8. Always state the unit explicitly — exam questions may ask for bits, bytes, or larger units.

Problem: A bitmap image is 640 pixels wide and 480 pixels tall with a colour depth of 24 bits per pixel. Calculate the file size in bytes.

Step 1 — File size in bits = 640 × 480 × 24 = 7,372,800 bits.

Step 2 — Convert to bytes: 7,372,800 ÷ 8 = 921,600 bytes.

Common mistakes: (1) Forgetting to multiply by colour depth — the question asks for colour depth separately for a reason. (2) Leaving the answer in bits when bytes are asked for. (3) Not stating ‘pixels’ as the unit for width and height — this is a marking point in its own right.

Sound Representation

Sound is an analogue signal — a continuous wave of changing air pressure. Computers cannot store continuous signals directly. Instead, sound is digitised by taking regular measurements called samples. Each sample captures the amplitude (volume level) at that instant.

Sample Rate and Bit Depth

Sample rate (also called sampling rate) is how many samples are taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz). A higher sample rate means more measurements per second, capturing the original wave more faithfully. The sample interval is the time between consecutive samples — it is the inverse of the sample rate. A sample rate of 44,100 Hz gives a sample interval of roughly 0.023 milliseconds.

Bit depth (also called sample resolution) is the number of bits used to store each sample. More bits means more distinct amplitude levels can be recorded. At 16-bit depth, \(2^{16} = 65,536\) distinct volume levels are possible per sample.

Key Fact

Sound file size (bits) = sample rate (Hz) × bit depth (bits) × duration (seconds). To convert to bytes, divide by 8. Increasing either sample rate or bit depth improves quality but increases file size.

Problem: A 30-second audio clip is recorded at 22,050 Hz with a bit depth of 16 bits. Calculate the file size in bytes.

Step 1 — Size (bits) = 22,050 × 16 × 30 = 10,584,000 bits.

Step 2 — Convert to bytes: 10,584,000 ÷ 8 = 1,323,000 bytes.

Limitations of Binary Representation

When the number of available bits is limited, binary representation becomes less precise. In images, fewer bits per pixel means fewer possible colours and visible banding or “colour blocking” in graduated tones. In sound, a lower bit depth means fewer amplitude levels, producing audible distortion known as quantisation noise. A reduced sample rate may miss rapid sound-wave variations, causing high-frequency detail to be lost.

These limitations represent the fundamental trade-off in data representation: more bits always means greater fidelity, but larger file sizes. Real systems manage this by choosing an appropriate bit width for the task — a voice call needs far less fidelity than a recording studio session.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Image file-size calculations are a reliable source of marks — but read the question carefully. State width and height in pixels (not “dots” or “points”) because the examiner expects the unit. If asked for the number of colours from colour depth \(d\), the answer is \(2^d\). For ASCII code calculations, always use the group starting point (A=65, a=97, ‘0’=48) and count from there — never guess.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • 7-bit ASCII represents 128 characters. Codes are sequential: A=65, a=97, ‘0’=48. Calculate any code by counting from the group start.
  • Bitmap image file size (bits) = width × height × colour depth. Always state width and height in pixels.
  • Sound file size (bits) = sample rate × bit depth × duration. Higher values of either setting improve quality but increase file size. Fewer available bits reduce fidelity.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the bit depth of a digital sound recording affects the quality and file size of the recording.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A higher bit depth means more bits per sample (1), so more distinct amplitude levels can be recorded (1), producing more precise volume measurements and higher-quality sound with less quantisation noise (1). More bits per sample increases the total file size because more data is stored per second (1).
Secure: Both effects described (quality improves, file size increases) with some supporting reason.
Developing: States quality improves and size increases but gives no mechanistic reason.
Emerging: One effect identified without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why binary representation of data has limitations when the number of available bits is restricted. Give examples from both images and sound.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fewer bits mean fewer distinct values can be represented (1). In images, a lower colour depth produces fewer possible colours and visible banding in gradual colour changes (1). In sound, a lower bit depth means fewer amplitude levels, causing audible distortion (quantisation noise) (1). A lower sample rate may also miss rapid changes in the sound wave, losing high-frequency detail (1).
Secure: One medium (image or sound) explained with two correct points.
Developing: Correct general idea (fewer bits = less accuracy) but no specific example developed.
Emerging: Vague — 'it will not be as good quality'.

lessons.title: Storage Units, File Sizes and Compression
lessons.description: KiB to TiB binary multiples, file-size calculations, and lossy vs lossless compression.
lessons.content_html:
Units of Data Storage

The smallest unit of data is a bit. Four bits make a nibble. Eight bits make a byte. For larger quantities of data, binary multiples are used. These are based on powers of 1024 (which is \(2^{10}\)) — not powers of 1000.

Key Fact

Binary multiples are based on 1024, not 1000:

  • 1 kibibyte (KiB) = 1,024 bytes
  • 1 mebibyte (MiB) = 1,024 KiB = 1,048,576 bytes
  • 1 gibibyte (GiB) = 1,024 MiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes
  • 1 tebibyte (TiB) = 1,024 GiB = 1,099,511,627,776 bytes

Why 1024, Not 1000?

Computer memory and storage are built from circuits that operate in powers of 2. A memory chip with address lines can access \(2^{10} = 1,024\) locations, not 1,000. Binary multiples therefore reflect the actual architecture of digital storage. The prefix “kibi” means \(2^{10}\), “mebi” means \(2^{20}\), “gibi” means \(2^{30}\), and “tebi” means \(2^{40}\). A tebibyte is therefore \(2^{40}\) bytes, or exactly 1,099,511,627,776 bytes.

Examiner reports highlight that many students confuse binary multiples with decimal SI prefixes (kB, MB, GB, TB, which use 1000-based steps) or cannot state how many bytes are in a tebibyte. Practise the 1024-step progression: bytes → KiB → MiB → GiB → TiB, each step multiplying by 1024.

Problem 1: A video file is 3,145,728 bytes. Express this in MiB.

Step 1: Convert bytes to KiB: 3,145,728 ÷ 1,024 = 3,072 KiB.
Step 2: Convert KiB to MiB: 3,072 ÷ 1,024 = 3 MiB.

Problem 2: A cloud storage server has 2 TiB of capacity. How many bytes is that?

Step 1: 1 TiB = 1,024 GiB, so 2 TiB = 2,048 GiB.
Step 2: 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB, so 2,048 GiB = 2,097,152 MiB.
Step 3: 1 MiB = 1,048,576 bytes, so 2 TiB = 2,097,152 × 1,048,576 = 2,199,023,255,552 bytes.
Alternatively: 2 × \(2^{40}\) = \(2^{41}\) bytes.

Key Fact

Every step up the binary multiple ladder multiplies by 1,024: 1,024 bytes = 1 KiB; 1,024 KiB = 1 MiB; 1,024 MiB = 1 GiB; 1,024 GiB = 1 TiB. A tebibyte is \(2^{40}\) bytes — over one trillion bytes.

Why Compression Is Needed

Data compression reduces the size of a file. Smaller files download faster, cost less to transmit and consume less storage. Without compression, a single high-definition video file could occupy several GiB — impractical for streaming at normal broadband speeds. A single uncompressed album of audio at CD quality would fill around 700 MiB; compressed to a common format it may occupy under 100 MiB.

Lossless Compression

Lossless compression reduces file size without throwing any data away. The compressed file is a mathematically equivalent representation of the original — decompressing it recovers the original exactly, with no differences whatsoever.

Lossless compression is essential whenever data integrity matters. Examples include text documents, program code, spreadsheets, database backups and medical scan images. If even one bit of a program file is altered by lossy compression, the program could crash or malfunction. The file format ZIP is a common lossless container. Image format PNG uses lossless compression. Audio format FLAC is lossless.

Lossy Compression

Lossy compression permanently removes some data to achieve a greater size reduction than lossless methods can deliver. The removed data is chosen to be the parts humans are least likely to notice — for images, this might mean merging similar colours; for audio, this might mean removing frequencies that the human ear struggles to detect at certain volumes.

Because the removed data is gone permanently, the original file can never be recovered exactly. However, for media such as photographs, music and video, the human perception system is forgiving enough that a well-compressed lossy file is indistinguishable from the original for most listeners and viewers. JPEG is a lossy image format. MP3 and AAC are lossy audio formats. Most video streaming uses lossy compression.

Lossless:

  • No data is permanently removed.
  • Original file can be perfectly restored.
  • Typically achieves a smaller reduction in file size than lossy methods.
  • Essential for text, program code, medical data, databases.
  • Example formats: ZIP, PNG, FLAC.

Lossy:

  • Data is permanently discarded.
  • Original cannot be exactly recovered.
  • Can achieve much greater size reductions than lossless.
  • Suitable for media (photos, music, video) where human perception fills gaps.
  • Example formats: JPEG, MP3, AAC, most streaming video.

Choosing Between Lossless and Lossy

The choice depends entirely on whether data integrity or file size is the priority. For a hospital storing patient scan images, lossless compression is mandatory — a lossy compression artefact could look like a clinical finding and lead to misdiagnosis. For a music streaming service, lossy compression is appropriate — the bandwidth saving is enormous and the quality loss is imperceptible at high bit rates.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For binary multiples, always use KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB (1024-based) — never kB/MB/GB/TB (1000-based). The examiner specifically awards marks for the correct unit abbreviation. For compression questions using the ‘Discuss’ command word, cover both lossless and lossy — including what each method does to the data, when each is appropriate and the trade-off between quality and file size. One-sided answers cannot achieve full marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Binary multiples are based on 1024: 1 KiB = 1,024 bytes; 1 MiB = 1,024 KiB; 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB; 1 TiB = 1,024 GiB. A tebibyte is \(2^{40}\) bytes.
  • Lossless compression removes no data — the original can be perfectly restored. Essential for program code, text and medical data.
  • Lossy compression permanently discards data to achieve smaller files. Suitable for media where human perception does not detect the loss. The original cannot be recovered.

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by lossless compression.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Lossless compression reduces file size (1) without removing any data, so the original file can be perfectly reconstructed (1).
Secure: Correct idea with one element missing.
Developing: Vague — 'the data is compressed without losing quality'.
Emerging: Confuses lossless with lossy.

practice_questions.text: A software company stores its source code files on a cloud server. Explain why lossless rather than lossy compression must be used when compressing these files.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Lossless compression preserves all data exactly (1), so the source code can be perfectly restored from the compressed file (1). Lossy compression permanently removes some data (1), so the restored code would differ from the original — potentially introducing bugs or making it impossible to compile and run (1).
Secure: Both types described with the consequence for code quality developed.
Developing: Identifies lossless is needed but only partly explains why.
Emerging: Vague reference to code needing to be accurate.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the use of lossless and lossy compression for storing and streaming video content. Refer to the trade-offs in quality, file size and suitability.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Lossless preserves every frame exactly — very large file sizes, appropriate for video editing masters where re-encoding must not degrade quality (1). Lossy can remove subtle differences between frames and colours the eye does not notice, achieving dramatic size reductions — essential for streaming where bandwidth is limited (1). Lossy quality loss is imperceptible at high bit rates for most viewers (1). For archiving or broadcast, lossless is preferred; for consumer streaming, lossy is standard (1). File size trade-off: lossy files may be 10× to 100× smaller than lossless for the same content (1). Conclusion: the choice depends on the intended use — streaming favours lossy; professional archiving favours lossless (1).
Secure: Four or five points covering both types with clear trade-off.
Developing: One type described fully, the other partially, with some mention of trade-off.
Emerging: One type described without discussing the other.
